title: UK Stablecoin Rules Take Shape: Bank of England Drops Holding Limits for a £40 Billion Issuance Guardrail, and the BoE and FCA Set Out How Systemic Issuers Will Be Jointly Regulated
summary: In June 2026 the Bank of England replaced proposed holding limits with a temporary £40 billion issuance guardrail per systemic stablecoin and cut required non-interest-bearing central bank deposits from 40% to 30% of backing; around June 30 it joined the FCA in setting out a two-part regime in which HM Treasury can recognise issuers as systemic.
description:
The United Kingdom has taken two significant steps in setting up its regulatory regime for stablecoins, digital tokens designed to hold a stable value, usually backed by reserves of conventional assets. In June 2026 the Bank of England published a policy statement and a draft Code of Practice for sterling-denominated systemic stablecoin issuers. Soon afterwards, the Bank and the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) set out how the two authorities will jointly regulate issuers that become systemic. Together they reveal a regime that is somewhat softer than first proposed.

The Bank's policy statement, dated June 22, 2026 according to PwC's summary, responds to a consultation the Bank launched in November 2025. Its most prominent change is to holding limits. The earlier proposal would have restricted how much of a systemic stablecoin an individual or business could hold, to protect banks from losing deposits too quickly. After feedback, the Bank dropped the holding limits. In their place is a temporary issuance guardrail of £40 billion per systemic stablecoin. PwC says the guardrail is not a trigger for systemic designation. Lewis Silkin's commentary adds that the Bank expects to remove the guardrail once it is satisfied that risks to credit provision have been effectively mitigated. Commentators regard the new approach as more workable than the old one, mainly because it drops individual holding limits.

The backing assets, the reserves that stand behind each token, were also changed. According to PwC, the share that must be held as non-interest-bearing deposits at the central bank falls from 40% to 30%, and the share that can be invested in short-term UK government debt rises to 70%. For issuers this matters because assets held at the central bank earn no interest, while government debt does, so a lower central bank share improves the economics of issuing a stablecoin. The Bank also plans a future Central Bank Liquidity Facility for eligible systemic issuers, which would give them access to liquidity in stress.

The draft Code of Practice covers backing assets and safeguarding, capital and reserves, issuance, legal claim and redemption, remuneration, and the temporary issuance guardrail. The consultation on it closes on September 22, 2026, and the Bank aims to finalise it by the end of 2026, after which it applies to recognised systemic issuers. Further guidance and supervisory expectations follow during 2027, and PwC reports that regulated stablecoins can operate in the UK from 2027.

The second step is the joint approach. In a document published around the end of June, which Lewis Silkin discussed on July 2, the Bank and the FCA explained that systemic issuers will not be in a wholly separate regime. The UK is building one integrated, two-part framework. The FCA regulates all UK-issued qualifying stablecoins and, in due course, their use in retail payments. If a stablecoin is widely used in payments and may pose risks to UK financial stability, HM Treasury may recognise its issuer as systemic, and the Bank and FCA then regulate it jointly. The Bank advises the Treasury, assessing each case holistically and looking forward, with factors that include scale, nature of use, substitutability, interconnectedness and the Bank's own use of the stablecoin in its monetary role.

An issuer can be recognised as "systemic at launch" if it is not yet at systemic scale but is likely to reach it. Non-systemic UK issuers stay within the FCA regime. Responsibilities differ: the FCA's rules address consumer protection, market integrity, competition and international competitiveness, while the Bank's requirements target financial-stability risks from stablecoins used as money at scale. The authorities aim to align requirements where appropriate, but full alignment is not expected, and systemic issuers should expect more stringent rules.

The approach document also covers transition. It explains which FCA rules continue after recognition, which may be disapplied, how Bank requirements are phased in and how supervision is allocated. PwC says firms may face transition periods of 12 to 36 months. The FCA and Bank will consult later this year on how FCA rules apply once the Treasury recognises a systemic issuer. Other regulators are involved case by case: the Prudential Regulation Authority where an issuer is part of a bank group, and the Payment Systems Regulator for payment systems it covers, though the FCA is expected to take over the latter's responsibilities.

The Code of Practice is still a draft, with a consultation open until September 22, and the further consultation on FCA rules is yet to come, so firms should treat the details as provisional.

The legal basis is the Financial Services and Markets Act 2023, which amended the Banking Act 2009 to extend the Bank's remit to digital settlement assets, including systemic stablecoins. The focus is sterling-denominated stablecoins, but the approach also covers non-sterling systemic stablecoins if their use becomes widespread in the UK.

For consumers, the immediate effect is limited: regulated stablecoins are not expected until 2027. For businesses considering issuing or accepting them, the message is to plan early for the systemic threshold, since partnerships and distribution can bring scale quickly. Lewis Silkin concludes that firms with plans to scale stablecoin payments should treat systemic regulation as a design consideration now.
source_name: PwC UK, Lewis Silkin and Bank of England/FCA publications (June-July 2026)
image_alt: Digital currency concept representing stablecoin regulation (illustrative)
key_points: The Bank of England's June 2026 policy statement drops proposed holding limits and replaces them with a temporary £40 billion issuance guardrail per systemic stablecoin, which is not a trigger for systemic designation.
Backing assets: the share held as non-interest-bearing central bank deposits falls from 40% to 30%, and up to 70% can be invested in short-term UK government debt, according to PwC's summary.
The FCA regulates all UK-issued qualifying stablecoins and later their use in retail payments; if HM Treasury recognises a stablecoin as systemic, the Bank and FCA regulate it jointly.
Firms moving from FCA-only supervision to joint oversight may face transition periods of 12 to 36 months, and the Bank plans a future Central Bank Liquidity Facility for eligible systemic issuers.
The consultation on the draft Code of Practice closes on September 22, 2026, the Bank aims to finalise it by the end of 2026, and regulated stablecoins can operate in the UK from 2027.
why_it_matters: Sterling stablecoins could become a mainstream payment method. The rules decide how much risk issuers can take with customers' money, how banks' lending is protected if deposits move into stablecoins, and whether the UK can attract issuers without risking financial stability.

title: AM Best Lifts Its Outlook on France's Non-Life Insurance Market to Stable From Negative, Saying Rate Increases Have Restored Profitability
summary: In a market segment report published around May 18, 2026, AM Best said continued rate increases are offsetting claims inflation and that the profitability of French non-life insurers has been restored, though it expects rate rises to continue at a reduced pace in 2026.
description:
A rating agency's view of the French non-life insurance market has improved. In a Best's Market Segment Report titled 'Market Segment Outlook: France Non-Life Insurance', published around May 18, 2026, AM Best revised its outlook on the segment to stable from negative. The change reflects what it describes as top-line growth and technical profitability. The facts below come from AM Best's press release as distributed by Business Wire. The page text did not state the date, but the press release address indicates May 18, 2026. The release as we read it gives no figures for premium growth, combined ratios or profits, so we do not provide any.

What did AM Best say? It expects premiums in the French non-life segment to keep growing over the next 12 months, driven by rate increases that offset continuing claims inflation. James Kenfack, a financial analyst at AM Best, said the overall profitability of the segment has been restored. He added: 'Positive rate adjustments are expected to continue in 2026, albeit at a reduced pace.' That is a notable qualification: prices are still rising, but more slowly. Morgane Hillebrandt, an associate director, said France is a highly competitive, mature market, and credited insurers' discipline, risk management and cost controls with helping to improve technical margins and sustain profitability. In plain terms, insurers raised prices, controlled costs and were selective about the risks they wrote, and the combination has worked.

How does that compare with the previous outlook? AM Best had a negative view for several years. A Reinsurance News report from June 2023 recorded the agency maintaining a negative outlook, and Business Wire headlines show the same stance being maintained in July 2025. The 2023 report gives the reasons. Real premium growth was expected to lag the economy, with premiums stagnant or shrinking after inflation. Insurers were competing hard to defend market positions, scale and margins, while government legislation and voluntary anti-inflation measures limited price increases. AM Best said then that 'the effect of higher losses and expenses is unlikely to be offset by comparable premium increases.' Claims costs and wage bills were rising, especially in motor insurance, and natural catastrophe losses from drought, hail and fire were causing consistent technical losses on catastrophe cover. The state-backed reinsurer Caisse Centrale de Réassurance guarantees the market, but not every event is covered, so private insurers bear some of the cost, and reinsurance costs were rising. The agency said the outlook could change if inflation eased and the market adjusted its pricing. The May 2026 revision suggests that this has happened, but the 2026 release as we read it does not describe the evidence in numbers.

The 2023 report also identified some strengths: motor insurance makes up only about a quarter of premiums, which helps stabilise the top line, and insurers were investing in insurtech and digital capabilities. We cite the 2023 report for context only; its figures and conditions are three years old.

What does a stable outlook mean? An outlook from AM Best is its view of the likely direction of the credit fundamentals of a market segment over the next 12 months. A stable outlook means AM Best expects the factors affecting the segment to stay broadly balanced, while a negative outlook means risks are tilted to the downside. It is not a rating of any one insurer, and it does not guarantee that individual companies will not be downgraded or upgraded. A negative outlook did not necessarily mean imminent downgrades, and equally a stable outlook does not mean none.

What are the risks that remain? The 2026 release, as we have it, does not list them. From the 2023 analysis, the structural issues in France are weather-related losses, competition in a mature market, and the cost of reinsurance, none of which has gone away. Our reading is that a stable outlook reflects improvement in profitability, not an end to those pressures.

How should the change be read alongside the 2023 picture? In 2023 the agency's concern was a squeeze: costs were rising faster than the premiums that insurers were allowed or able to charge. In 2026 its language is about the opposite balance, in which rate rises are large enough to offset claims inflation. That does not mean claims costs have stopped rising; the release still refers to ongoing claims inflation. What changed is the gap between prices and costs, and the agency now sees that gap as closed enough for the segment to be profitable. It also expects the pace of rate increases to slow, which is consistent with a market where the repair has largely been done. The release does not say what would cause the outlook to change again, so readers should treat it as a snapshot of the next 12 months and not as a long-term forecast.

What does it mean for policyholders? Rate increases are continuing at a slower pace, according to AM Best, which suggests that French households and businesses should not expect large price falls, but may see smaller rises than in previous years. Profitability that has been restored gives insurers more room to compete, though competition in a mature market can also push prices down if claims stay benign. The release does not forecast prices for customers.

For readers who follow the sector, the useful next steps are to look at the full AM Best report, which is available to subscribers, and to watch insurers' results for combined ratios and the cost of weather events. This article is a news summary and not insurance or investment advice.
source_name: AM Best (Best's Market Segment Report, via Business Wire) and Reinsurance News
image_alt: Insurance policy review representing non-life insurance sector outlook (illustrative)
key_points: AM Best revised its outlook on France's non-life insurance segment to stable from negative in its Market Segment Outlook published around May 18, 2026.
The agency expects premiums to keep growing over the next 12 months, driven by rate increases that offset ongoing claims inflation.
Analyst James Kenfack said overall profitability has been restored and that 'positive rate adjustments are expected to continue in 2026, albeit at a reduced pace'.
Associate director Morgane Hillebrandt called France a highly competitive, mature market and credited insurers' discipline, risk management and cost controls for better technical margins.
The earlier negative outlook, maintained for years, reflected stagnant real premiums, rising claims costs, natural catastrophe losses and higher reinsurance costs.
why_it_matters: A rating agency's segment outlook is a signal about how safe and profitable an insurance market is expected to be. A move from negative to stable suggests the pressure of the past few years on French home, motor and business insurers has eased, although it does not remove the risk from weather and competition.

title: Allianz Agrees to Buy HSBC Life Singapore for S$2.7 Billion With a 15-Year Exclusive Bancassurance Deal, Beating Sumitomo Life and Daiichi Life
summary: Allianz Asia Holdings agreed on July 24, 2026 to buy HSBC Life (Singapore) outright for S$2.7 billion (about US$2.1 billion), paired with a 15-year exclusive bancassurance agreement and a S$200 million upfront payment, with completion expected in the first half of 2027 subject to MAS approval.
description:
German insurer Allianz has won the contest for HSBC's life and health insurance business in Singapore. Insurance Business reported on July 24, 2026 that Allianz Asia Holdings is acquiring HSBC Life (Singapore) outright from HSBC Insurance (Asia-Pacific) Holdings for S$2.7 billion, equivalent to about US$2.1 billion or £1.6 billion. The announcement settles what earlier press reports had described as a race in which Allianz was the frontrunner and in which HSBC was reported to be seeking a valuation of up to about US$2 billion.

The agreement has two parts. The first is the purchase of the company. The second is a 15-year exclusive bancassurance agreement, in which HSBC's branches will sell Allianz protection, health, retirement and wealth products to customers in Singapore. Allianz is paying an upfront S$200 million for the distribution rights. Bancassurance is the practice of selling insurance through a bank's customer network, and for an insurer it can be more valuable than the policies already on the books because it provides access to a stream of new customers. A long exclusive contract is meant to protect that stream.

Completion is expected in the first half of 2027 and depends on approval by the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS). That timetable means HSBC Life will continue to operate under HSBC ownership for several more months, and customers will not see changes to their policies on the announcement date. Existing policies would normally continue on the same terms after an ownership change.

For HSBC, the sale is a financial and strategic step. The bank expects a pre-tax gain of roughly US$1.8 billion and a boost to its core capital ratio of up to 15 basis points, which is 0.15 percentage points. HSBC Life Singapore posted a pre-tax profit of S$118 million for 2025. HSBC's London-listed shares rose by more than 1% after the news, while Allianz shares moved only marginally in early trading. HSBC is not leaving insurance distribution: its branches will continue to sell Allianz products under the new agreement.

For Allianz, the deal is a significant expansion in a market it has tried to enter on a larger scale before. In 2024, the insurer walked away from a roughly S$2.2 billion bid for a majority stake in Income Insurance, formerly NTUC Income, after public criticism and government scrutiny. The HSBC target is a foreign bank's subsidiary rather than a cooperative-rooted local insurer, which may make the transaction less politically sensitive, although the article does not say so. Allianz says it has a regional presence of roughly a century, operates in eight Asian markets and has around 9 million customers, and the acquisition makes Singapore one of its largest life and health markets in Asia. Chief executive Oliver Bäte called Singapore "central to our global growth strategy", and board member Renate Wagner said the deal aims "to support more individuals and communities even more comprehensively."

Competition was real. Insurance Business says Sumitomo Life and Daiichi Life were reported as rivals, and that in mid-June it had reported Allianz outbidding them for a business then valued at up to US$2 billion. The article does not give the rivals' bid amounts. A later Insurance Business report, on October 16, noted that Allianz beat Sumitomo Life to HSBC's Singapore life business, and that Sumitomo Life is looking for deals in the United States and Southeast Asia, naming Income Insurance as a possible target.

The market backdrop is positive. Bloomberg Intelligence analyst Steven Lam expects Singapore's life insurance new business to grow at least 15% this year, according to the article. Rising incomes, an ageing population and high savings rates make life, health and retirement products attractive. That growth, together with the profit figure of S$118 million for HSBC Life, helps explain the price. At S$2.7 billion, it is about 23 times the 2025 pre-tax profit, although part of the price is for the exclusive 15-year distribution agreement and not just for the profits of the existing business, so a simple multiple overstates what is paid for earnings alone.

The article does not state premium volumes or customer numbers for HSBC Life Singapore, so it is not possible to describe the size of the book beyond its profit. Nor does it describe how the S$2.7 billion will be financed.

What should readers watch? The MAS approval is the main milestone. Integration will matter for customers and staff, particularly how Allianz handles the move from HSBC's brand and systems, and how well HSBC's sales force adapts to selling a partner's products under an exclusive arrangement. In the wider market, the deal signals that bancassurance contracts remain highly valued, and that foreign insurers are willing to pay high prices to secure distribution in Singapore. It also underlines the position of Singapore as a hub where global insurers want a presence, as the Monetary Authority's work on new risk-transfer structures such as protected cell companies suggests.
image_alt: Singapore skyline representing insurance sector deals (illustrative)
key_points: Allianz Asia Holdings is acquiring HSBC Life (Singapore) outright from HSBC Insurance (Asia-Pacific) Holdings for S$2.7 billion, about US$2.1 billion.
The deal includes a 15-year exclusive bancassurance agreement with an upfront payment of S$200 million, under which HSBC branches will sell Allianz protection, health, retirement and wealth products.
Completion is expected in the first half of 2027, subject to approval from the Monetary Authority of Singapore.
HSBC expects a pre-tax gain of roughly US$1.8 billion and a core capital ratio boost of up to 15 basis points; HSBC Life Singapore made a 2025 pre-tax profit of S$118 million.

Sumitomo Life and Daiichi Life were reported as rival bidders, and in 2024 Allianz had walked away from a roughly S$2.2 billion bid for a majority stake in Income Insurance after public criticism and government scrutiny.
why_it_matters: Singapore is one of Asia's richest life and health insurance markets, and bank-sold insurance is a major channel. The deal makes Allianz a much bigger player there, shows how global insurers compete for distribution through banks, and simplifies HSBC's portfolio.

title: Ontario Blue Cross Launches 'Rainy Day' Cover, Canada's First Weather-Triggered Travel Insurance, Paying $100 for Each Covered Rainy Day
summary: Announced on June 18, 2026, the add-on pays $100 per covered rainy day by Interac e-Transfer within two business days when rainfall at the destination passes the contract's threshold, with no claim to file; it must be bought at least 14 days before departure.
description:
A Canadian health insurer has launched a travel insurance add-on that pays out when it rains. Ontario Blue Cross announced Rainy Day coverage on June 18, 2026 and describes it as the first weather-based travel insurance product of its kind in Canada. The facts below come from the company's press release and from an Insurance Business Canada report published the same week. The release says the cover is available online. It does not name an underwriter, state the premium or give the rainfall threshold, and the press coverage did not either, so those details are missing from this article and buyers should confirm them in the policy wording. Amounts are in Canadian dollars.

How does it work? Parametric insurance, which is the category this belongs to, pays a fixed amount when an objective, measurable event occurs, without the insured having to show how much loss they suffered. Here the measurable event is rainfall at the traveller's destination. According to the release, automated weather monitoring tracks conditions during the trip. If rainfall at the insured destination exceeds the threshold set in the contract and all the conditions of cover are met, the traveller is notified and invited to claim compensation. Insurance Business Canada describes an algorithm that monitors rainfall and triggers the payout when precipitation passes the contractual threshold, with policyholders notified automatically. The two descriptions differ slightly, since one says travellers are invited to claim and the other that notification is automatic, so readers should check how the process works in the contract. The release says no proof is required and no claim needs to be filed.

What is the payout? The coverage pays $100 per covered rainy day, per contract. Payment is made by Interac e-Transfer within two business days. The release does not say whether there is a cap on the number of days or on the total payout, so we cannot say what the maximum is. To put the amount in perspective, $100 will not cover the cost of a ruined holiday, and the product does not attempt to: Insurance Business Canada describes it as a complement to traditional travel insurance and not a replacement, aimed at the gap between a spoiled holiday and a covered financial loss. A traditional policy pays for specific losses such as cancelled trips or emergency medical bills. This product pays a small, predictable amount for a frustration that traditional policies do not cover.

Who can buy it, and when? It is an add-on, available only with Emergency Medical Care, Trip Cancellation and Interruption, or the 3-in-1 Package. The eligible destinations are Mexico, Cuba, the Dominican Republic, the United States, Canada and Europe. The coverage must be bought at least 14 days before departure, which prevents customers from buying cover when they already know the forecast. The release does not describe exclusions or other conditions, so it is not possible to say, for example, how a 'rainy day' is defined, whether it is a calendar day or 24 hours of rain, or which weather station is used.

Why would an insurer offer this? Ontario Blue Cross's Anne-Gaëlle Le Hénaff, Vice-President of Commercialization, said the company is turning 'a common travel frustration into a tangible benefit for travellers.' Insurance Business Canada argues that parametric products reduce claims-handling costs, because no one has to assess a loss, and that this is what makes small payouts like $100 per rainy day viable at scale. It also notes that industry observers say take-up of such products remains far from mass adoption. That caution is worth keeping in mind: a novelty product has to be understood by customers before it sells.

What should a traveller consider? First, whether the trigger matches what you care about. A threshold set by a weather station may not match the weather where you are staying, and rain that spoils your day might not meet the contract's threshold. Second, whether the cost of the add-on is reasonable for a payout of $100 a day, which we cannot judge because the premium was not published. Third, whether it overlaps with other cover. It does not replace trip cancellation or interruption insurance, which reimburse costs when a covered event stops your trip. Fourth, the destination list excludes many popular places, so check that yours is included. As general background, parametric products have a feature called basis risk: the payout may not match the real loss, and you can lose out when it rains and you are paid nothing, or be paid when you did not mind the rain.

For the insurance industry, the interest is that parametric models, which have been more common in agriculture and catastrophe cover than in everyday consumer products, are now reaching leisure travel. Whether other insurers follow will depend on customers' response. Readers should read the policy wording from Ontario Blue Cross before buying. This article is a summary of a product launch and is not insurance advice.
source_name: Ontario Blue Cross (press release of June 18, 2026) and Insurance Business Canada
image_alt: Rainy airport window representing weather-based travel insurance (illustrative)
key_points: Ontario Blue Cross announced Rainy Day coverage on June 18, 2026, calling it the first weather-based travel insurance of its kind in Canada.

Automated weather monitoring tracks rainfall at the insured destination; if it exceeds the threshold in the contract and the coverage conditions are met, the traveller is notified and paid $100 per covered rainy day, per contract.
No proof of loss is needed and no claim has to be filed; payment is by Interac e-Transfer within two business days.

It is an add-on to Emergency Medical Care, Trip Cancellation and Interruption, or the 3-in-1 Package, for trips to Mexico, Cuba, the Dominican Republic, the United States, Canada and Europe, and must be bought at least 14 days before departure.
The release does not state the premium, the rainfall threshold in millimetres, a cap on days or the underwriter, so buyers need to read the contract wording.
why_it_matters: Parametric insurance pays on a measured event, not on proof of loss, so it can pay fast and cheaply. A small consumer product like this shows how insurers may use weather data for everyday risks, and it shows what buyers should check: the trigger, the payout and the conditions.
